passage: On the school trip bus in Lisbon, Paulo's head jerked sideways and he made a small hooting sound. Two boys in the seat ahead turned round and stared. Then one of them jerked his own head and hooted, and they both laughed. Paulo looked out of the window. His throat felt tight. He wished he could make himself small enough to disappear. Liam, sitting beside him, didn't turn round to the boys, and he didn't whisper "ignore them." He just kept holding out the packet of crisps. "Which dinosaur are we seeing first? I vote the big one." When they got off, the teacher had a quiet word with the two boys. Liam walked beside Paulo into the museum, still talking about teeth.

qa.q: What did Liam keep holding out to Paulo?
qa.a: The packet of crisps.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel when the boys copied him, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt hurt and embarrassed; he looked out of the window with a tight throat, wishing he could disappear.

qa.q: Which choice by Liam helped Paulo most, and why?
qa.a: He simply carried on as normal, sharing crisps and chatting about dinosaurs, so Paulo felt ordinary, not like a problem.

qa.q: How might the two boys see Paulo after the teacher's quiet word?
qa.a: They may realise the movements and sounds are not a joke or a choice, and stop copying him.

grounding: It shows a child with tics hurt by stares and mimicking, with a teacher stopping the mocking and a seatmate who carries on as normal.

passage: During silent reading, Pradeep grunted twice, loudly. Half the class spun round. Someone at the back grunted back, and giggles spread. Pradeep gripped his book so hard the page tore. His eyes stung. He had been trying to hold it in for ten whole minutes. Hafsa Ma'am closed her book. Her voice was calm but firm. "Eyes on your own pages. Pradeep has tics. They're sounds and movements his body makes that he doesn't choose, the way you don't choose a hiccup. Copying them is unkind, and it stops now." The room went quiet. Then Nivedita, next to Pradeep, slid her bookmark over so he could fix the torn page, and went on reading. At lunch Pradeep sat with her, and nobody grunted.

qa.q: What did Nivedita slide over to Pradeep?
qa.a: Her bookmark, so he could fix the torn page.

qa.q: What does Pradeep gripping his book so hard that the page tore show?
qa.a: It shows how hurt and tense he felt when the class laughed, after trying to hold in the sounds for ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Hafsa Ma'am's brief explanation change in the room?
qa.a: It made clear the tics weren't a choice and stopped the mocking, so the room went quiet.

qa.q: How does Nivedita's way of reacting differ from the back row?
qa.a: She simply helped with the torn page and carried on reading, treating Pradeep normally instead of laughing.

grounding: It shows a child with tics hurt by stares and mimicking, a teacher who briefly explains it is not a choice and stops the mocking, and a classmate who carries on normally.

passage:
Thursday
Today in maths Manoj copied my head jerk and made the squeaky sound I make. Four boys laughed. I wanted the floor to swallow me. I can't stop it. I told Mumma once, it's like trying not to sneeze.
Then Lata Ma'am put down her chalk. She said, "Rashmi's movements are tics. They are not a choice. Nobody in this class copies them again." That's all she said. Then she went back to fractions. Manoj went red.
At lunch Pooja sat next to me and just talked about her cousin's wedding like nothing happened. She didn't look at my head at all. I ate my whole tiffin.
I still feel sore inside. But less.

qa.q: What did Lata Ma'am say about Rashmi's movements?
qa.a: She said they are tics, not a choice, and nobody in the class copies them again.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Manoj copied the head jerk?
qa.a: Rashmi felt humiliated and hurt, wishing the floor would swallow her.

qa.q: Why did Lata Ma'am's response work well?
qa.a: It was brief, stated clearly that tics are not a choice, stopped the mocking and then moved on without making a fuss.

qa.q: How does Pooja seem to see Rashmi at lunch?
qa.a: Pooja seems to see Rashmi simply as a friend, not as the tics, chatting about the wedding as if nothing happened.

grounding: Shows a child hurt by a classmate's mimicking of tics, helped by a teacher's brief explanation and a friend who carries on as normal.

passage: At the bus stop outside the village school near Mandi, two boys jerked their heads sideways every time Charu, eleven, did. They laughed and nudged each other. Charu stared at her shoes, blinking fast, her chest aching. Sharma Sir, walking to his scooter, stopped. "Charu's movements are not something she chooses. Copying her is cruel, and it ends today." The boys shuffled off. Charu's friend Kalyani didn't mention it at all. She just kept telling Charu about the calf born in their cowshed that morning, how it slipped on the straw and stood up again. By the time the bus came, Charu was laughing about the calf, too.

qa.q: What was born in Kalyani's cowshed that morning?
qa.a: A calf was born in the cowshed that morning.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when the boys copied her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, staring at her shoes with her chest aching.

qa.q: What did Sharma Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He briefly explained that the movements are not a choice, called the copying cruel and stopped it on the spot.

qa.q: How does Kalyani seem to see Charu?
qa.a: Kalyani sees Charu as an ordinary friend to chat with; she never mentions the movements and just talks about the calf.

grounding: Shows a child hurt by mimicking of her tics, helped by a teacher who explains they are not a choice and a friend who simply carries on.

passage: In a Manchester primary school, Bilal, ten, cleared his throat loudly, a tic that came in bursts. During silent reading a girl turned and stared, then another. Someone whispered, "Is he doing it on purpose?" Bilal hunched over his book, face hot. Ms Clarke looked up. "Bilal has tics. His body does them without him choosing, a bit like hiccups. Eyes on your own books, please." The staring stopped. At break Tomas, his friend, handed him the football as usual. "You're in goal first." He didn't mention it at all. Bilal dived for every shot until the bell, and forgot all about the reading room.

qa.q: What did Ms Clarke compare Bilal's tics to?
qa.a: She compared them to hiccups.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel when classmates stared during silent reading?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, hunching over his book with a hot face.

qa.q: Why was Ms Clarke's explanation helpful?
qa.a: It was short and clear, said the tics are not a choice and turned the class's attention back to their own books.

qa.q: How does Tomas treat Bilal at break, and what does it show?
qa.a: Tomas hands him the football and puts him in goal as usual, showing that Bilal is simply his friend.

grounding: Shows a child hurt by stares at his tics, helped by a teacher's brief explanation and a friend who carries on as normal.

passage:
In Class 5B, Arohi's head jerked sideways and a small squeak came out of her throat. Three children turned to stare. At the back, Kabir jerked his own head and squeaked, and a few kids laughed.
Arohi stared hard at her notebook. Her eyes stung.
Mrs Rekha, the class teacher, put down her chalk. "Kabir, stop. Class, Arohi's body sometimes makes movements and sounds she doesn't choose. It's like hiccups. Nobody laughs at hiccups. We carry on." Her voice was calm but firm, and she went straight back to the lesson.
At break, Tara sat next to Arohi as usual and talked about her cat's new kittens, as if nothing had happened. Arohi's head jerked once. Tara just kept talking. Slowly, Arohi started to smile.

qa.q: What did Tara talk about at break?
qa.a: Her cat's new kittens.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when Kabir copied her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and humiliated, staring at her notebook with stinging eyes.

qa.q: Which responses helped Arohi, and why?
qa.a: Mrs Rekha's brief explanation that it isn't a choice and her firm stop to the mocking, plus Tara carrying on as normal, made Arohi feel safe and ordinary.

qa.q: What would change if Mrs Rekha had ignored Kabir's mimicking?
qa.a: The class might think mocking was acceptable, and Arohi would feel even more alone and exposed.

grounding: Arohi is hurt by stares and mimicking of her tics; a teacher explains briefly and stops the mocking, and a friend carries on as normal.
